title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution consumed 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate of paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the sealed design, execution accounting, representative examples, contamination‑check evidence (10% Mininet holdout → 20 tasks; contamination summary records zero disagreements), and an artifact‑grounded discussion of operational implications and threats to validity (preregistration id: cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02).

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation with generative language models promises operational productivity gains but risks incorrect or unsafe changes that can cause outages, policy violations, or degraded service. Prior proposals therefore integrate LLM generation with deterministic validators and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR) so that unsafe candidates can be detected and corrected before application. The operational value of automated repair depends on (i) the baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures produced by the chosen generator/prompting policy; (ii) the validator’s coverage and fidelity; and (iii) the repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness. We asked a narrowly scoped, preregistered confirmatory question: Does a deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce the incidence of validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank?

Contributions. (1) A sealed preregistered paired design (n = 200) that enforces shared‑initial generation semantics to isolate the effect of applying a deterministic validator+repair to the same generated candidate. (2) A fully archived autonomous execution with deterministic reconciliation and concrete accounting (completed pairs = 200, model_calls_used = 200, repair_calls = 0). (3) An honest, artifact‑grounded null/degenerate confirmatory outcome and interpretation that clarifies when automated repair can and cannot reduce validator‑detected failures, together with reproducibility notes and operational recommendations grounded in the archived artifacts.
sections.related_work: LLMs exhibit factual errors and prompt sensitivity across domains; mitigation approaches include grounding (retrieval augmentation), verifier‑assisted repair, and bounded/guarded agent architectures. Prototype NetOps systems demonstrate that intent→configuration synthesis is feasible but often lack instrumented, production‑like failure‑rate studies. Architectural proposals combine LLM generation with deterministic network validators (e.g., Batfish or domain checkers) and repair loops to improve safety; empirical red‑team and configuration‑brittleness studies show that tool‑description injection and tool‑chaining can materially change safety outcomes. Surveys and prototype evaluations motivate externally auditable, preregistered measurements that isolate the marginal effect of adding deterministic repair for a fixed model and prompt policy. Our study situates itself among generator→validator→repair proposals and external‑evaluation critiques by measuring a prespecified paired estimand under tightly controlled, archived conditions.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and inferential plan. The study was preregistered as cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02 with a paired design (n = 200 tasks), a single pre‑registered primary test (exact McNemar two‑sided, α = 0.05), and a model‑call cap of 400 (one initial generation per task plus up to one repair call if the validator failed). The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and the primary inference used an exact McNemar test; 95% confidence intervals were computed with a bootstrap percentile method (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Power planning assumed a baseline unsafe incidence ≈ 30% and a target 50% relative reduction; detailed planning and stopping rules were frozen prior to execution in the preregistration.

Task bank and validators. We used a curated, machine‑checkable intent→configuration bank of 200 tasks spanning four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge; 50 tasks each). Each task encodes initial and expected final states, workflow constraints (for example: make‑before‑break, must_be_down_for_fields patterns), and an explicit required_sequence. The primary deterministic checker (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforces intent/constraint rules and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as a secondary disagreement detector applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to detect validator–emulator mismatches; the run executed that holdout and the analysis artifact analysis/contamination_summary.csv records zero disagreement flags.

Model, generation semantics, and adapter enforcement. The experiment used the hosted model declared in the preregistration (gpt‑5‑mini) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. Crucially, the adapter enforced shared_initial generation semantics: for each task the system produced a single initial candidate (preregistered deterministic sampling policy) which was then reused for both baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (GVR) conditions. This design choice isolates the effect of validator+repair on the same generator output and removes per‑condition sampling variance. The adapter accounting shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, confirming shared reuse across conditions.

Repair policy, budgets, and contamination handling. The preregistered repair policy allowed one automated repair prompt to the same LLM per task when the primary validator reported violations; up to 200 repair calls were therefore allowed but only if the initial candidate failed validation. The contamination_plan deterministically excluded tasks where primary validator vs emulator disagreed; sensitivity analyses were preregistered to include flagged tasks as failures or successes. Missingness and exclusion rules were fixed in advance and applied deterministically during execution.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and descriptive outcome. The autonomous run completed all planned episodes: completed_episode_count = 400 (shared initial generation reused across conditions) and complete_pair_count = 200. Model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued. Condition summaries (analysis/condition_summary.csv) show baseline successes = 200/200 and guarded successes = 200/200 (success_rate = 1.0 for both). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0.

Primary inferential result. With zero discordant pairs the observed paired difference estimate = 0.0. The exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.0]. Under the preregistered estimand and test the prespecified ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis is logically untestable on this sample because there were no baseline validator failures for GVR to reduce.

Repair activity and contamination checks. Because no initial candidate failed deterministic_netops_validator_v5, the GVR pipeline applied zero repair prompts and incurred zero repair‑call cost. The preregistered Mininet holdout (10% → 20 tasks) executed as recorded; the analysis artifact analysis/contamination_summary.csv reports no validator–emulator disagreements. Deterministic reconciliation artifacts report all consistency checks passed (pair_accounting_consistent = true, episode_accounting_consistent = true). Provider call accounting shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, cache_miss_count = 200, cache_hit_count = 0, reflecting the shared_initial generation design that produced a single generator invocation per task which was deterministically reused across conditions.

Representative examples and diagnostics. Representative task artifacts (for example, pair‑000001 through pair‑000006) show shared initial generator outputs that precisely matched the task required_sequence and passed validation: validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true and violation_count = 0 in each representative record. Representative difficulty annotations (e.g., make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change) and parsed_command_count/required_command_count are recorded in the validator traces and verify that tasks exercised medium‑to‑very_hard workflow constraints despite producing validator‑satisfying candidates.

Planned sensitivity checks and unexecuted branches. The preregistration contained sensitivity analyses to handle flagged contamination and alternative missingness treatments; because no tasks were flagged and no episodes failed, these sensitivity branches were not invoked. Secondary/exploratory estimands (average repair iterations, GVR‑introduced failure rate, model‑call cost per successful repair) are not reported because no repair attempts occurred; the analysis bundle records these secondary_results as empty.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The observed degenerate confirmatory outcome demonstrates a logical point: when the chosen model, prompt policy, and adapter produce validator‑passing candidates for all items in a workload, a validator‑coupled repair step cannot reduce validator‑detected failures. This null result is tightly scoped: it does not imply GVR is never useful. Instead, it shows that GVR’s marginal operational benefit is conditional on baseline validator failure prevalence and on validator coverage.

Why baseline failures were zero. Artifact‑grounded explanations include: (1) the prompt template and shared_initial semantics produced candidates that conformed to the explicit task‑bank constraints; (2) the curated task bank encodes workflows with clear required_sequences that map directly to validator checks and may therefore be easier for a deterministic prompt policy to satisfy; (3) the primary validator enforces the task‑encoded constraints but may omit certain end‑to‑end device behaviors that only an emulator or real device could reveal; and (4) the single repair budget combined with the shared_initial design removes per‑condition re‑sampling as a pathway for generating alternative, repairable candidates.

Operational implications. Before investing in automated repair automation, practitioners should measure baseline validator failure prevalence on representative workload distributions and examine validator coverage with end‑to‑end emulation. When baseline validator failures are low, resources may be better spent on extending validator fidelity (richer device semantics, vendor idiosyncrasies), adversarial testing, multi‑model or multi‑sample generation, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals. Conversely, when baseline failures are non‑negligible, GVR can reduce validator‑detected issues; realized gains will depend on repair budget, repair prompt engineering, and validator completeness.

Reproducibility note and gap. All key execution artifacts (model‑call logs, validator traces, paired contingency tables, bootstrap parameters) are archived in the execution bundle and referenced in the analysis artifacts. The analysis/contamination_summary.csv reports zero disagreements for the Mininet holdout (10% → 20 tasks). One remaining reproducibility gap is the absence of a labeled artifact recording the randomized selection seed for the Mininet holdout; that seed is not present with an explicit label, which prevents exact reconstruction of the drawn holdout despite the contamination summary evidence of zero disagreements. We report this gap transparently and include the contamination summary evidence that no disagreements were observed.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: preregistration, deterministic adapter enforcement, and frozen stopping rules protect against post‑hoc design changes; however, the shared_initial design trades generality for control and specifically removes per‑condition sampling variance. Construct validity: the primary validator checks the task‑encoded constraints but may omit device‑level or vendor idiosyncratic failure modes only visible under end‑to‑end execution. External validity: evaluation used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini), a single sampling policy (shared initial), and a curated task bank; results may differ across model families, sampling temperatures, multiple draws, larger repair budgets, or adversarial distributions. Conclusion validity: the planned McNemar test is uninformative when discordant pairs are zero; nonetheless reporting the observed zero‑discordance outcome is an operationally meaningful datum that should inform future workload selection and power planning.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and ran a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs). The preregistered hypothesis of a ≥50% relative reduction in validator‑detected unsafe changes was not testable on this task bank because the baseline failure rate was 0%. This outcome emphasizes that the marginal value of automated repair is workload dependent: when baseline validator failures are rare, repair yields no measured benefit for validator‑detected errors. Future work should measure GVR value on workloads with nontrivial baseline failure prevalence, extend validator fidelity with richer emulator or real‑device checks, evaluate multi‑sample and multi‑model generation policies, and explore multi‑step or human‑in‑the‑loop repair budgets to characterize practical operational gains. All execution artifacts, logs, and analysis outputs are archived for independent inspection.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (mandatory). This study executed under the autonomous post‑lock preregistration cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02 and used the hosted model declared as gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family. The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Topic constraints: the human Research Director limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes. Frameworks and tools: code and experiment orchestration used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 framework and the deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5). The primary deterministic validator was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (intent/constraint checks). A Mininet‑based emulator served as the preregistered secondary disagreement detector applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks). Preregistration and freeze: the experimental plan (estimand, sample size n = 200, paired design, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair call budget = 1 per task, shared‑initial generation semantics) was frozen before any model calls. Autonomous execution and artifacts: the run executed autonomously under the frozen plan; model calls, prompts, seeds, validator traces, emulator traces, logs, and the artifact manifest are archived in the execution bundle. Model‑call budget and usage: 200 model calls were used (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were allowed but none were applied because initial candidates passed the validator. Human involvement: the human Research Director selected the topic family and pre‑lock constraints; no human manual editing or selective rewriting of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred. Known reproducibility gap: the explicit randomized holdout selection seed used for the Mininet contamination check is not present as a labeled artifact in the archived bundle; this absence prevents deterministic reconstruction of the exact holdout selection despite the contamination summary reporting no disagreements. The master prompt archive reference above is the immutable prompt required by the track.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested (execution artifacts record hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts shared_initial_generation = 200). Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
